# Objectively Good Tea

https://marshaln.com/2017/12/objectively-good-tea/

*December 12, 2017*

---

A friend of mine had a grandmother who loved drinking wine.

However, she didn't drink wine the normal way.

She drank nice red wines with ice—actual ice cubes in the glass. Even expensive vintage Bordeaux.

You can imagine the horror of the people serving the wine, but when an elderly woman wants her wine that way and doesn't care what you think—and she's paying—you serve it that way.

I think we can generally agree that this is probably a suboptimal way of serving wine. Nobody serious in the wine industry would recommend putting ice cubes in fine wine. Most people also wouldn't ask for it, because they know it would sound odd.

Most of us, whether we admit it or not, care at least somewhat about what other people think. Asking for ice in a fine wine can make you look rather silly.

---

## Brewing Oolong with Cooler Water

I bring this up because of a discussion in a Facebook tea group about brewing oolongs with cooler water.

My position is fairly simple:

Brewing oolongs with water that isn't close to boiling is a waste of tea.

It's similar to putting ice cubes in wine. It dilutes the experience and prevents the tea from expressing itself fully.

If you're paying good money for high-quality leaves and brewing them at 85°C, you're essentially leaving value behind.

---

## The Argument for Lower Temperatures

The most common argument is that lower temperatures reduce problems such as:

* Bitterness
* Sourness
* Astringency

This is true.

However, lower temperatures also reduce extraction.

In tightly rolled modern oolongs, water below boiling may require two or three infusions before the leaves fully open. Everything extracts more slowly.

As a result, you either:

1. Extend steeping times, or
2. Accept a weaker brew.

The end result is often a flatter and less interesting tea.

Like ice in wine, you're avoiding some negatives but also sacrificing many positives.

---

## Skill Matters More Than Temperature

This isn't to say you can't enjoy tea that way.

If you genuinely prefer it, go ahead. It's your tea and your money.

However, personal preference doesn't mean there isn't a best way to brew a tea or an objective way to evaluate one.

When you become skilled at brewing, bitterness, sourness, and astringency cease to be major problems. You learn to manage them through:

1. Leaf-to-water ratio
2. Infusion timing
3. Adjustments from cup to cup

The brewer remains in control.

Using cooler water may help avoid mistakes, but it also limits the tea's maximum potential. The better solution is simply to improve your brewing skills rather than handicap the tea with warm water.

---

## Tea Is More Than Immediate Flavor

Another factor rarely discussed in English-language tea circles is that many tea drinkers—particularly in Chinese tea culture—evaluate tea on more than just the flavor present when swallowing.

Lasting fragrance and aftertaste matter enormously.

When I drink tea at the office, one of my favorite experiences is driving home half an hour later and still tasting the tea in my mouth.

The aftertaste lingers.

With poor-quality tea or weak brewing, that rarely happens.

A pleasant floral flavor at the moment of drinking can be enjoyable, but one of the key distinctions between a good tea and a great tea is how long it stays with you.

That effect generally requires stronger brewing.

Only then can you fully appreciate what the tea has to offer.

---

## Why Tea Competitions Use Boiling Water

This is also why tea competitions and commercial grading systems use standardized brewing methods with boiling water.

After tasting enough tea, experienced evaluators quickly learn to distinguish stronger teas from weaker ones.

One of the most important indicators is how much a tea has to give.

The deeper, richer, and more persistent the flavor, the higher the quality tends to be.

Competition brews are often:

* Bitter
* Strong
* Intense
* Not especially pleasant to drink casually

However, good teas reveal a kinder side beneath that intensity. They leave behind complexity, depth, and a lasting aftertaste.

Poor teas are simply bitter and thin.

---

## Preference vs. Quality

Personal taste matters.

Some people will always prefer one tea over another, even if objective measures suggest the second tea is higher quality.

The analogy I used in that Facebook discussion was simple:

Some people will always prefer a Big Mac over a carefully made gourmet burger prepared with exceptional ingredients.

Individual preference doesn't eliminate the possibility that objective standards exist.

You can enjoy whatever you like while still acknowledging that some teas possess greater depth, complexity, and quality than others.
